Read the measurements in context

Every completed trial stayed within two rotations per public insertion and four per public deletion. The deletion totals include both internal refreshes.

Parallel isolated C++ subprocesses on a shared host; other benchmark suites may run concurrently. Wall times include scheduling and contention; process CPU times exclude descheduling but still reflect the shared machine. Neither is a single-core latency or comparative speedup claim. Compare timings within that execution context. The height and rotation observations describe these seeded workloads; the mathematical guarantee is a separate argument; see the explained proof in Downloads.

Filters tables and traces; highlights its curves.

Random churn

Retire original keys in a seeded shuffled order and insert fresh keys in increasing order. The live set stays close to its starting size.

Ascending churn

Delete the original keys in increasing order and insert increasing fresh keys. This keeps the live set close to its starting size.

Descending churn

Delete the original keys in decreasing order and insert decreasing fresh keys. This tests the reverse direction of the increasing refresh sweep.

Shrink and regrow

Delete every original key, reaching an empty tree, then insert a new set of the same size. Extra checkpoints record the small-tree stages.

Read-heavy churn

Retire original keys in shuffled order and insert increasing fresh keys. Add eight lookups per replacement: four successful and four unsuccessful.

Largest completed size in each workload

Each row uses that workload's own largest completed size; check the starting-key count before comparing. Means show ± sample SD when repeated seeds exist. Maximum heights and rotation maxima are observed extrema, not means.

How the experiment was measured

  • The measured strategy is geometric-full-bst, with p = 3/4. A successful deletion that leaves keys refreshes two keys in sorted cursor order. A sweep wrap moves the minimum directly to the root; this pointer move is counted separately from rotations.
  • Each trial starts with n live keys. Preloading, capacity reservation, operation generation and structural validation are outside the update timer. Internal refreshes, their searches and random trials, and operation-statistics accumulation are inside it.
  • The four update-only workloads perform n deletions and n public insertions: 2n measured operations. Read-heavy churn adds 8n lookups, giving 10n operations. Its time-per-operation denominator therefore includes cheaper lookups; it is not a direct comparison of deletion speed.
  • Parallel isolated C++ subprocesses on a shared host; other benchmark suites may run concurrently. Wall times include scheduling and contention; process CPU times exclude descheduling but still reflect the shared machine. Neither is a single-core latency or comparative speedup claim. Wall time includes scheduling delays. Process CPU time excludes time waiting for the CPU, but both measurements can reflect shared memory and cache contention. These are concurrent-run measurements, not isolated throughput rankings.
  • For repeated seeds, each chart point is the arithmetic mean and whiskers are ± one sample standard deviation. The table uses the same convention. A single seed has no variability estimate. Neither standard deviations nor these finite samples establish a high-probability theorem.
  • Root depth is zero. Final mean depth averages all stored nodes. “Max final H” is the largest final height across the recorded seeds. “Sampled max H” is the largest height at the validation checkpoints, including the preloaded tree; it is not the maximum after every update.
  • The height ratio uses the final live size: H/log₂(n + 1). Each trace shows live size and height together, including the empty stage during shrink and regrow. Empty-tree height is -1, drawn at zero in the trace. Lines between checkpoints are visual guides, not additional observations.
  • Insert/delete rotation averages divide by the corresponding public operation counts. Refresh reinsertions are charged to deletion. Peak RSS covers the entire worker process, including input generation, preload and validation, so it is larger than node-array storage alone.
  • Completed trials pass the worker's structural and key-set checks at the recorded checkpoints. Failed and skipped trials remain in the data and are never replaced by zeros. The source archive, seeds and recorded configuration make the workloads reproducible.
